lessons.title: Test-Driven Development (TDD) Core Cycles
lessons.description: Write tests before code — the Red-Green-Refactor cycle produces cleaner, more reliable software.

sections.heading: The TDD cycle
paragraphs: Test-Driven Development flips the normal workflow: you write a failing test first, write the minimum code to make it pass, then refactor. This cycle repeats for every feature.
list: Red — write a test that fails (no implementation yet)
Green — write the simplest code that makes the test pass
Refactor — clean up the code while keeping tests green
Repeat for each new feature or edge case

codeExamples.heading: TDD in action
explanation: Write the test first — it describes exactly what you want.
The test fails initially because the function doesn't exist.
Write just enough code to pass the test.
Refactor only if the code needs improvement.

practice.task: TDD a multiply function: write the test first, watch it fail, then write the function to pass it.
hints: Implement: function multiply(a, b) { return a * b; }.
Add more test cases for edge cases: 0, negative numbers.

keyTakeaways: TDD: Red (failing test) → Green (passing code) → Refactor (clean up).
Write tests first — they define the desired behavior.
Write the minimum code to pass — don't over-engineer.
Refactor only when tests are passing — safety net catches regressions.
lessons.challenge: TDD a divide function that handles division by zero, returning Infinity for 0 denominator.

lessons.title: Writing Test Suites: describe, it, expect Assertions
lessons.description: Organize tests with describe blocks and verify behavior with expect assertions.

sections.heading: Test structure
list: describe("name", () => {}) — groups related tests
it("description", () => {}) — defines a single test case
expect(value).toBe(expected) — checks equality
Vitest/Jest provide the testing framework and assertion library

sections.heading: Common matchers
list: toBe() — strict equality (===)
toEqual() — deep equality for objects/arrays
toBeTruthy() / toBeFalsy() — truthiness checks
toContain() — checks if array/string contains a value
toThrow() — checks if a function throws an error

codeExamples.heading: Test suite with assertions
explanation: describe groups tests for a specific class or feature.
it defines individual test cases with descriptive names.
expect().toBe() checks for exact value equality.

practice.task: Write a test suite for a Calculator class with add, subtract, multiply and divide methods. Include at least 3 test cases per method.
hints: Each method gets its own describe block.
Test normal cases, edge cases and error cases.

keyTakeaways: describe groups related tests; it defines individual test cases.
Use descriptive test names that explain the expected behavior.
matchers like toBe, toEqual and toThrow verify different aspects of behavior.
A good test suite covers normal cases, edge cases and error conditions.
lessons.challenge: Write a complete test suite for a shopping cart with addItem, removeItem, getTotal and applyDiscount methods.

lessons.title: Testing Asynchronous Logic & Promise Rejections
lessons.description: Test async functions, Promises and error handling in asynchronous code.

sections.heading: Testing async code
list: Use async/await in test functions for clean async tests
Test Promise rejections with rejects
Mock timers with vi.useFakeTimers() for setTimeout/setInterval
Test fetch with mock servers or interceptors

codeExamples.heading: Async testing patterns
explanation: Use async in the test function to await async operations.
.rejects.toThrow() verifies that a Promise rejects with a specific error.
Fake timers let you control setTimeout/setInterval without waiting.
Always restore real timers after using fake ones.

practice.task: Write tests for an async function that fetches data, including tests for success, network failure, and timeout scenarios.
hints: Mock fetch with vi.fn() to simulate responses.
Test success: mock returns { ok: true, json: () => data }.
Test failure: mock returns { ok: false }.

keyTakeaways: Use async/await in test functions for clean async test code.
Fake timers let you control time-dependent code in tests.
Mock external dependencies to test in isolation.
lessons.challenge: Write tests for a retry function that attempts an operation up to 3 times before failing.

lessons.title: DOM Testing using JSDOM / HappyDOM Environments
lessons.description: Test DOM manipulation code without a real browser using lightweight DOM implementations.

sections.heading: DOM testing environments
paragraphs: JSDOM and HappyDOM provide a lightweight implementation of the DOM in Node.js. This lets you test code that manipulates HTML elements without opening a browser.
list: JSDOM — full DOM implementation in JavaScript, slower but complete
HappyDOM — lighter and faster alternative to JSDOM
Both provide document, window, and DOM APIs in Node.js
Configure via your test framework's environment setting

codeExamples.heading: Testing DOM manipulation
explanation: The @vitest-environment comment sets the DOM environment.
beforeEach clears the DOM between tests for isolation.
Create DOM elements and interact with them just like in a browser.
Verify element content with expect and standard matchers.

practice.task: Write DOM tests for a toggle button that adds/removes a 'dark' class on the body when clicked.
hints: Create the button programmatically or set innerHTML.

keyTakeaways: JSDOM and HappyDOM let you test DOM code without a real browser.
Always clear the DOM between tests for isolation.
Simulate user interactions by calling methods like .click() directly.
DOM tests verify that your code correctly creates and manipulates elements.
lessons.challenge: Write tests for a todo list app that creates, completes, and deletes items — all using DOM testing.
